title: Certainty and intention to create legal relations
subtitle: When an agreement is too vague to enforce, and when the parties never meant the law to enforce it at all
objectives: Explain why an agreement that is too vague or incomplete to give it a workable meaning will fail for uncertainty
Distinguish a court filling a genuine gap by implication from a court rewriting the parties' bargain
State and apply the presumptions governing intention to create legal relations in domestic/social and commercial settings, and identify how each can be rebutted

leadingAuthorities.citation: RTS Flexible Systems v Molkerei Alois Muller [2010] UKSC 14
leadingAuthorities.role: A binding contract can arise from certain, performed terms even where a formal 'subject to contract' document was never signed
Silence on a mechanic does not defeat an otherwise workable agreement where a term can be supplied by implication
Domestic and social agreements are presumed not intended to be legally binding
The domestic presumption is rebutted once spouses deal at arm's length after separation
Commercial promises are presumed intended to be binding; an 'ex gratia' label does not by itself rebut that

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students treat offer and acceptance as the whole test for a contract and stop there. Where the profile shows understanding running ahead of knowledge of the presumptions, this note appears: 'You can usually spot a deal forming — this lesson is about the two ways a deal can form and still not be enforceable.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the RTS and Balfour rules cold on paper. The test pool below leans on fact patterns — expect scenarios where you have to decide which presumption applies before you can decide anything else.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Slow down through Parts 1 to 4 and hold onto the five case names as you go — Part 5 assumes you can say, without prompting, which presumption each one illustrates.

overview.hook: Two companies work together for months, delivering machinery, sending invoices, paying them — all on the strength of a letter that begins 'Subject to contract: usual terms to be agreed.' Then something goes wrong, and one side insists there was never a contract at all. Were they right? The answer turns on two separate questions English law asks of every agreement: is this deal certain enough to enforce, and did the parties actually mean the law to be able to enforce it?
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 22 September 2026. The doctrines of certainty and intention to create legal relations are settled common law, refined by later authority rather than displaced by it.

parts.heading: When 'we agree in principle' isn't an agreement
parts.voice: conversational — opens with an everyday failed negotiation before naming the doctrine
body: Suppose two businesses agree the big things — price, goods, delivery date — but leave one detail hanging: 'usual terms to be agreed.' If those usual terms are never actually pinned down, is there a contract at all? The starting point in English law is unforgiving: an agreement that is too vague, or missing a term essential to working out what either side is actually bound to do, is not a contract. Courts enforce bargains, not intentions to strike one later.

But 'too vague to enforce' is a narrower category than most students assume. Courts lean hard against letting an agreement collapse for uncertainty, especially once the parties have acted on it as though it were binding — paying invoices, delivering goods, performing services. Unpicking months of performance because of a loose phrase in a covering letter would defeat the whole point of contract law, which is to hold people to bargains they have actually struck.

RTS Flexible Systems v Molkerei Alois Muller shows how far that reluctance goes. The parties negotiated a contract for packaging machinery under a letter of intent expressly stated to be 'subject to contract' — meaning no binding agreement was meant to exist until a formal contract was signed. No formal contract was ever signed. The parties nonetheless kept working: Muller took delivery, RTS carried out and was paid for further work, and both sides operated exactly as though a deal existed. When a dispute later arose, the Supreme Court held a binding contract had come into existence regardless — the 'subject to contract' label had, in substance, been overtaken by conduct, and the terms the parties had actually been working to were certain enough to enforce.

components.caseName: RTS Flexible Systems v Molkerei Alois Muller
components.factsShort: Negotiations for a packaging line were conducted under a letter of intent stated to be 'subject to contract'; no final contract was ever signed, but both parties performed fully as though bound.
components.ratioShort: Where parties have acted on terms sufficiently certain to be enforced, the absence of a final signed document — even one expressly 'subject to contract' — will not by itself prevent a binding contract arising.

expanded.facts: RTS agreed to design, build and install an automated packaging line for Muller. A letter of intent set out core commercial terms and capped RTS's liability, but stated the parties intended to enter a full written contract, and that until then the arrangement was 'subject to contract'. The letter of intent expired, but the parties carried on: RTS built and delivered the equipment, Muller took delivery and paid substantial sums, and both sides continued to negotiate the outstanding fine detail without ever executing the final document. A dispute arose over defects, and Muller argued no contract existed at all, so RTS's liability cap (found only in the unsigned draft) did not apply.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Supreme Court held that the parties' conduct after the letter of intent expired was inconsistent with an understanding that they remained free of contractual obligation. Applying an objective test of what a reasonable observer would conclude from the parties' words and conduct, the Court found the 'subject to contract' qualification had been discarded, and that the terms actually being performed — including the liability cap — were sufficiently certain to be given contractual effect.
expanded.significance: RTS is the leading modern statement that certainty and formality are different questions. A missing signature does not automatically mean a missing contract; what matters is whether an objective observer, looking at what the parties actually did, would say they intended to be bound on ascertainable terms.

interaction.prompt: Two businesses perform a deal for months under a letter marked 'subject to contract', with no final agreement ever signed. Can a binding contract still exist?
options: Yes — if the parties' conduct shows the label was superseded and the terms are certain enough to enforce
No — 'subject to contract' always prevents a binding contract forming, whatever the parties do afterwards
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. RTS shows formality and certainty are separate questions — conduct can overtake a 'subject to contract' label if the terms being performed are certain enough to enforce.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. 'Subject to contract' is a strong signal against a binding deal, but RTS shows it isn't an absolute bar — sustained performance on certain terms can displace it.

parts.heading: Filling a silence, not rewriting a bargain
parts.voice: forensic — dissects a single ruling clause by clause
body: Wells v Devani starts with an informal phone call. Mr Devani, an estate agent, told Mr Wells he could find a buyer for a block of flats in return for a commission if he introduced a purchaser who went on to buy. Neither man specified exactly when that commission would become payable — on introduction, on exchange of contracts, or on completion. Wells sold to the buyer Devani introduced, then refused to pay, arguing the agreement was too uncertain to be a contract at all, because it never said when the money was due.

The Supreme Court did not ask whether every term had been spelled out. It asked whether the missing term could be supplied by implication from what the parties evidently intended — here, that commission would fall due on completion, the point at which a sale is treated as achieved in the ordinary course of an estate agent's business. Supplying that term did not require the court to guess at anything; it required only that the court recognise what both men plainly assumed without saying it.

That distinction — implication versus invention — is the whole doctrine in miniature. A court may fill a genuine silence if the missing term would have gone without saying to these parties, had an officious bystander interrupted the negotiation to ask. What a court may never do is supply a term the parties never turned their minds to at all, dressed up as 'implication', because at that point the court is not completing the parties' bargain — it is making a new one for them. Where the gap really is that kind of gap, no amount of judicial goodwill saves the agreement: it was simply never made.

components.factsShort: An estate agent orally agreed a commission for introducing a buyer, without specifying when the commission became payable; the agent later found a buyer, but the seller refused to pay.
components.ratioShort: An essential but unstated term can be supplied by implication where it reflects what the parties evidently intended, rather than a term the court has invented to rescue an incomplete bargain.

expanded.facts: Devani told Wells, in an unstructured telephone conversation, that he would find a buyer for Wells's block of flats for a 2% commission if his introduction led to a sale. He introduced a buyer, who went on to complete the purchase. Wells refused to pay commission, arguing that because the parties never specified the contingency that would trigger payment — introduction, exchange, or completion — the agreement was too uncertain to amount to a binding contract.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The majority held that the natural reading of the parties' exchange was that commission would be payable on completion, since that is the point at which a sale is normally treated as concluded in estate agency practice. The absence of an express term on timing did not defeat the contract, because a workable term could be implied to reflect what both parties evidently understood, rather than requiring the court to construct new terms for them.
expanded.significance: Wells v Devani confirms that certainty is judged generously where a sensible, implied answer to the missing question is available. It sits alongside RTS as authority that English courts try hard to hold parties to bargains they plainly meant to make, rather than let informality or incompleteness defeat them.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below, adapted from the reasoning in Wells v Devani, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
interaction.passage: The agreement did not expressly state when commission became payable. However, the natural inference from the parties' exchange, read in the context of ordinary estate agency practice, was that commission would fall due on completion of the sale. A term to that effect could properly be implied to give effect to what the parties evidently intended, rather than to impose an obligation neither party had contemplated. The agreement was accordingly sufficiently certain to be enforced.
interaction.ratioSentence: A term to that effect could properly be implied to give effect to what the parties evidently intended, rather than to impose an obligation neither party had contemplated.

parts.heading: Promises between people who trust each other anyway
parts.voice: wry — treats the domestic cases with a knowing, faintly ironic tone
body: Balfour v Balfour is the case every contract student remembers slightly wrong. Mr Balfour, working abroad, promised his wife £30 a month while he was away; the marriage later broke down, and she sued him for the unpaid sums. On the face of it, an offer, an acceptance, even a kind of consideration. The Court of Appeal still found no binding contract — because agreements between spouses living together in amity are presumed not to have been intended to carry legal consequences at all.

The reasoning is less sentimental than it sounds. It isn't that the court thought Mr Balfour's promise was insincere; it's that treating every arrangement inside a functioning household as a contract — who does the washing up, who pays for the shopping, who promised whom a lift to the station — would flood the courts and turn ordinary family life into a standing set of legal obligations nobody actually wants enforced. The presumption exists to keep the law out of the kitchen, not to doubt anyone's word.

Merritt v Merritt is the same relationship producing the opposite result, and the contrast is the point. By the time the Merritts made their agreement, the marriage had already broken down and the husband had moved out. He agreed in writing that if his wife kept up the mortgage payments on the house, he would transfer it into her sole name. When he later refused, she sued and won. The presumption against intention simply did not apply here: the parties were no longer living together in amity, they were negotiating their separate interests at arm's length, and — tellingly — they wrote it down. Same institution, same surnames on the paperwork, entirely different legal result, because the assumption underneath the presumption — mutual trust standing in for legal enforcement — had already broken down along with the marriage.

components.factsShort: A husband promised his wife a monthly allowance while working abroad; the marriage later broke down and she sued to enforce the promise.
components.ratioShort: Agreements between spouses living together in amity are presumed not to be intended to create legal relations, because domestic arrangements are not the kind of thing the parties mean the courts to police.

interaction.prompt: Two scenarios. In which is a court most likely to find an intention to create legal relations?
interaction.scenarioA: A husband and wife, living together and on good terms, agree that he'll handle the household bills while she covers the grocery shopping.
interaction.scenarioB: A separated couple, negotiating through solicitors, sign a written agreement that the wife will pay off the remaining mortgage in exchange for the husband transferring the house into her name.
interaction.explanation: B mirrors Merritt: the couple are no longer living in amity, they are dealing at arm's length over their separate financial interests, and the agreement is in writing. A mirrors Balfour: an informal division of household responsibilities between spouses living together attracts the domestic presumption against legal enforceability.

parts.heading: In business, the presumption flips
parts.voice: brisk — commercial, efficient, no wasted words
body: Move the same question into a business context and the default answer reverses. Edwards v Skyways involved a pilot made redundant by his airline. The airline wrote to him promising an 'ex gratia' payment roughly equivalent to his accrued pension contributions, if he agreed to withdraw from the company pension scheme. He agreed. The payment was never made in full, and the airline argued the word 'ex gratia' showed it never intended the promise to be legally binding.

It lost. Commercial agreements carry a strong presumption that the parties intend legal relations, and it takes clear words to displace that presumption — not vague or informal language, and not a label chosen for its own reasons. 'Ex gratia' has a specific, narrower meaning in this context: it signals that the payer makes no admission of any pre-existing legal liability to pay. It says nothing about whether the fresh promise now being made is itself meant to bind. The pilot was entitled to the money.

Treat the commercial presumption as genuinely strong, not a formality to tick off. Rebutting it takes an express statement that legal relations are not intended — a clause stating, in terms, that an arrangement is binding in honour only, for instance — not merely informal drafting, a friendly tone, or a payment described as gratuitous. Absent words that actually do that work, a business promise is taken to mean what it says.

components.factsShort: An airline promised a redundant pilot an 'ex gratia' payment if he withdrew from the pension scheme, then failed to pay the full amount, arguing the label showed no intention to be bound.
components.ratioShort: The commercial presumption in favour of intention to create legal relations is strong; a phrase like 'ex gratia', which addresses liability rather than bindingness, does not by itself rebut it.

components.term: 'Ex gratia' is not a magic word
components.definition: In this context, 'ex gratia' means the payer admits no pre-existing legal duty to pay. It does not mean the new promise being made is non-binding — those are two different statements, and only the second one rebuts the commercial presumption.

interaction.prompt: In Edwards v Skyways, why did describing the payment as 'ex gratia' fail to rebut the presumption of intention to create legal relations?
options: Because the word was in Latin, and only English terms can exclude legal effect
Because 'ex gratia' denies a pre-existing legal liability, not the bindingness of the new promise being made
Because commercial promises can never be non-binding, whatever words are used
interaction.trapExplanation: Students often reach for the third option — treating the commercial presumption as absolute. It is only a presumption, and can be rebutted by clear words. The point in Edwards is narrower: 'ex gratia' simply isn't that kind of clear word, because it addresses a different question.

parts.heading: Two presumptions, one underlying question
parts.voice: dialectic — sets the two presumptions against each other and resolves the tension
body: Strip away the labels and both presumptions are answering the same question from opposite starting points: would a reasonable person, looking at this exchange, think the parties meant the law to be able to step in and enforce it? Domestic and social context suggests probably not, because the relationship itself usually does the enforcing. Commercial context suggests probably yes, because businesses generally want their promises to count for something. Neither is a rule; both are starting presumptions that evidence can move.

The domestic presumption moves when the underlying relationship of trust has broken down and the parties are negotiating at arm's length instead — that's Merritt. It also moves, in the other direction, wherever the stakes or formality of a domestic-looking arrangement are high enough that the parties plainly did mean business — courts have found intention in serious financial arrangements between family members even without a formal separation, where the facts show real bargaining rather than mutual goodwill.

The commercial presumption moves the other way only on genuinely clear evidence — an express statement that a document is not to be legally binding, for example. It is not moved by informality, generosity, or a promise described in gratuitous-sounding terms, as Edwards v Skyways shows. The single most common mistake in this area is treating either presumption as a rule rather than a starting point: ticking 'commercial, therefore automatically binding' or 'family, therefore automatically not' without asking whether anything in the facts actually rebuts it.

components.title: Intention to create legal relations: a decision path
components.description: A flowchart for working out which presumption applies and whether it has been rebutted.

nodes.label: Is the context domestic/social, or commercial?
Domestic/social → presumption AGAINST intention to be legally bound
Commercial → presumption IN FAVOUR of intention to be legally bound
Is there evidence the parties dealt at arm's length (e.g. separation, writing, serious financial stakes)?
Is there clear, express language excluding legal effect?

components.textAlternative: First classify the context as domestic/social or commercial. Domestic/social carries a presumption against intention to be legally bound, which is rebutted by evidence of arm's-length dealing such as separation, a written agreement, or serious financial stakes. Commercial carries a presumption in favour of intention to be legally bound, which is rebutted only by clear, express language excluding legal effect. In each branch, if the presumption is rebutted the agreement is binding; if it stands, it is not.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that silence on an essential mechanic — such as exactly when a payment falls due — always makes an agreement too uncertain to enforce?
interaction.explanation: Wells v Devani shows silence on a mechanic is not fatal where a sensible term can be implied from what the parties evidently intended. Uncertainty only defeats an agreement where the gap cannot be filled this way — where it reflects something the parties genuinely never agreed at all.

testPool.prompt: State the basic requirement of certainty an agreement must satisfy before a court will enforce it as a contract.
acceptableAnswers: the terms must be certain enough to be given a workable meaning
the agreement must not be too vague or incomplete to enforce
testPool.modelAnswer: An agreement must be certain enough — its essential terms ascertainable, whether expressly or by sensible implication — for a court to be able to say what each party is actually bound to do.

testPool.prompt: In RTS Flexible Systems v Molkerei Alois Muller, did the fact that no final contract was ever signed prevent a binding contract from arising?
options: No — the parties' performance on certain terms was enough despite the missing signature
Yes — a signed final document is always required once a letter of intent says 'subject to contract'

testPool.prompt: Why does the law presume that agreements between spouses living together in amity are not legally binding?
options: Because such promises are usually made insincerely
Because treating every domestic arrangement as an enforceable contract would be unworkable and unwanted by the parties themselves
Because spouses cannot, as a matter of law, contract with one another
testPool.trapExplanation: The presumption is not a comment on sincerity, and spouses plainly can contract with each other, as Merritt shows. The real justification is practical: courts and the parties themselves don't want ordinary household arrangements treated as a web of enforceable obligations.

testPool.prompt: Put these steps in the order a court follows when deciding whether a missing term can be filled by implication rather than defeating the agreement for uncertainty.
items: Identify the term the parties left unstated
Ask whether that term would have gone without saying to these parties at the time
If yes, supply the term to reflect what was evidently intended
If no, treat the gap as a genuine failure to agree and hold there is no contract on that point

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, adapted from Merritt v Merritt, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
testPool.passage: The parties were husband and wife, but by the time of the agreement they had separated and were no longer living together in amity. Their arrangement over the house was recorded in writing and reached through negotiation over their now-separate financial interests. Where spouses deal with each other at arm's length in this way, the presumption against an intention to create legal relations does not apply, and the ordinary approach to commercial and personal agreements governs instead. The agreement was therefore binding.
testPool.ratioSentence: Where spouses deal with each other at arm's length in this way, the presumption against an intention to create legal relations does not apply, and the ordinary approach to commercial and personal agreements governs instead.

testPool.prompt: A written clause reads: 'This agreement is not entered into as a formal or legal agreement, and shall not be subject to legal jurisdiction in the courts.' What does language like this achieve that the word 'ex gratia' in Edwards v Skyways did not?
options: It expressly excludes legal enforceability, which is the clear language needed to rebut the commercial presumption
It merely denies a pre-existing legal liability, like 'ex gratia' did
It has no legal effect at all in a commercial contract

testPool.prompt: Two neighbours, on friendly terms, agree that one will water the other's plants while she's on holiday, in exchange for the returning favour next summer. On these facts alone, is this presumed to be a legally binding contract?
options: No — an informal social arrangement between neighbours attracts the presumption against intention to create legal relations
Yes — because each side promised to do something for the other
testPool.explanation: A mutual promise alone is not enough; this is a social arrangement of the kind Balfour's reasoning is aimed at, and nothing here rebuts the presumption against legal intention.

testPool.prompt: A supplier and a retailer exchange emails settling price, quantity and delivery dates for a bulk order, adding only 'full terms to follow'. The retailer takes delivery and pays the first invoice before a dispute arises over the missing terms. Is the agreement likely to fail for uncertainty?
options: Not necessarily — performance on the agreed core terms, as in RTS, points towards an enforceable contract despite the loose phrase
Yes — any unresolved phrase like 'full terms to follow' automatically defeats certainty
testPool.explanation: As in RTS, conduct consistent with a concluded deal on ascertainable core terms weighs heavily against letting an unresolved phrase sink the whole agreement.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that most clearly rebuts the domestic presumption in this scenario.
testPool.scenarioText: A brother and sister, close but living separate lives, put in writing a formal agreement, drafted with the help of a solicitor, that the sister will invest a fixed sum in the brother's business in exchange for a fixed share of future profits.
tappableSpans: put in writing a formal agreement
drafted with the help of a solicitor
testPool.correctSpan: drafted with the help of a solicitor
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Solicitor involvement, alongside the written, formal, investment-style terms, is strong evidence the parties intended a genuine legal bargain rather than a family favour — exactly the kind of arm's-length dealing that rebuts the domestic presumption.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact most inconsistent with an informal family favour. Formal written terms are relevant, but professional legal drafting is the clearest signal that this was meant to bind.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario more closely mirrors Edwards v Skyways than Balfour v Balfour?
testPool.scenarioA: A company writes to a departing employee promising a goodwill bonus 'as a gesture of appreciation', which the employee relies on in agreeing to waive a separate claim.
testPool.scenarioB: A father tells his adult daughter, still living at home, that he'll give her extra pocket money if she helps around the house more.
testPool.explanation: A is a commercial-adjacent promise from an employer, attracting the presumption in favour of intention, and 'as a gesture of appreciation' does no more rebutting work than 'ex gratia' did in Edwards. B is a domestic arrangement within a household, attracting the opposite presumption.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that the presumptions governing intention to create legal relations are fixed rules rather than starting points?
testPool.explanation: Both presumptions are exactly that — presumptions. Merritt rebuts the domestic one; Edwards shows how hard it is, but not impossible, to rebut the commercial one. Treating either as an automatic rule is the most common error in this topic.

testPool.prompt: Two colleagues verbally agree to split any winnings from a weekly office lottery pool they run informally, with no written record and no money changing hands beyond small weekly contributions. One week, one colleague buys a ticket alone and wins, then refuses to share it. Analyse whether the other colleague can enforce the sharing agreement.
factsToOrder: The agreement was made verbally between colleagues, not in a formal business context
The arrangement was informal and social in character, run for fun rather than as a business venture
Small weekly contributions were made, but this is consistent with a social pool rather than a commercial venture
One colleague later refuses to honour the sharing arrangement

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the colleagues intended their informal lottery-sharing arrangement to be legally binding.
modelAnswer.rule: Social and informal arrangements attract a presumption against intention to create legal relations; the presumption can be rebutted by evidence of arm's-length, business-like dealing, but mere financial stakes are not enough on their own.
modelAnswer.application: Although money changes hands, the arrangement is informal, verbal, unwritten and run for fun among colleagues rather than as a genuine commercial venture — closer to Balfour's reasoning than to a business deal. Nothing here — no writing, no formal structure, no professional involvement — points towards the kind of arm's-length dealing that rebutted the presumption in Merritt or sustained it in Edwards.
modelAnswer.conclusion: On these facts, the presumption against intention to create legal relations is unlikely to be rebutted, and the sharing arrangement is probably not enforceable as a contract.

testPool.prompt: A student argues that because a letter of intent said 'subject to contract', no binding contract could ever arise, regardless of anything the parties did afterwards. What is wrong with this argument?
options: It correctly states the law — 'subject to contract' is an absolute bar
It treats a strong indicator against intention as an unbreakable rule, ignoring that sustained performance on certain terms can override it, as in RTS
'Subject to contract' has no legal significance at all
testPool.trapExplanation: 'Subject to contract' is genuinely powerful evidence against a binding deal, which is what makes the trap tempting. RTS shows it is not conclusive: an objective view of the parties' later conduct can show the label was abandoned in substance.

testPool.prompt: A freelance designer and a small business orally agree a project fee and deadline, adding 'we'll sort the finer details as we go'. The business pays a deposit and the designer starts work. Is the core deal likely too uncertain to enforce?
options: No — the essential terms (fee, scope, deadline) are fixed, and conduct on those terms supports enforceability despite loose language about details
Yes — any phrase suggesting details remain open always defeats certainty

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating the domestic and commercial presumptions as fixed rules rather than rebuttable starting points — assuming 'family' always means unenforceable and 'business' always means binding, without checking whether the facts actually rebut the presumption in play.
